Boyd Gaming's Q3 Revenue Slips to $990.5M as Las Vegas Destination Travel Softens

Published November 1, 2026 · 4 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Boyd Gaming reported third-quarter 2026 revenue of $990.5 million, a slight decline from roughly $1.0 billion in the same quarter last year, as softer destination travel to Las Vegas — concentrated at its Orleans property — weighed on results even as locals play and the company's online business kept growing.

The numbers

Net income for the quarter came in at $124.9 million, or $1.71 per share. That's down sharply from the prior-year quarter's reported $1.4 billion, or $17.81 per share, but that comparison is skewed: the 2025 quarter included a $1.4 billion after-tax gain from the sale of Boyd's equity stake in FanDuel, along with $65.1 million in non-cash impairment charges on long-lived assets, neither of which recurred this year. Adjusted EBITDAR for the quarter was $319.6 million, down modestly from $321.8 million a year earlier. The company also returned close to $180 million to shareholders through buybacks and dividends during the quarter.

Where the softness showed up

CEO Keith Smith said quarterly results were "impacted by increased softness in destination business to Las Vegas, primarily affecting our Orleans property," while noting the company remains "encouraged by the continued strength of our Las Vegas locals portfolio." On the earnings call, Smith described the destination slowdown as intensifying through the year, with July holding up, August weaker than expected, and September improving slightly on August. He pointed to ongoing room renovations at the Orleans — more than 300 rooms out of service for the past year — as a factor, saying the property would have its full room count back online in the current quarter. Outside of Las Vegas, Boyd's Midwest and South segment grew once one-time items like last year's Sam's Town Tunica closure and this year's Sam's Town Shreveport sale were stripped out, and the company's online business, led by its Stardust-branded casino app, posted double-digit Adjusted EBITDAR growth.

Why it matters

Boyd's results add to a pattern showing up across the Las Vegas Strip and off-Strip operators this earnings season, with destination visitation running softer than locals-driven and online business. For bettors and casino players, that broader slowdown has already shown up in state-level revenue reports and in competitors' own Q3 results, and it's a reminder that a casino operator's headline revenue swings can reflect one-time accounting items — like last year's FanDuel sale gain — as much as they reflect the underlying health of the gaming business.
